claim: In rich media, bacteria such as E. coli and Bacillus subtilis may have a doubling time shorter than the duration of DNA replication.
source: In rich media, bacteria such as E. coli and Bacillus subtilis may have a doubling time shorter than the duration of DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on bacterial DNA replication.

claim: Bacteria achieve doubling times shorter than DNA replication duration by having several ongoing rounds of DNA replication, each initiating from the single oriC locus on the chromosome.
source: This remarkable feat is achieved by having several ongoing rounds of DNA replication, each initiating from the single oriC locus on the chromosome, most of which will only terminate in a future generation (Yoshikawa and Sueoka, 1963; Yoshikawa et al., 1964).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yoshikawa and Sueoka, 1963 and Yoshikawa et al., 1964.

claim: Bacteria initiate new rounds of DNA replication in a synchronous fashion, with the number of origins of replications doubling within a time frame that is short compared to the cell cycle duration.
source: In contrast to eukaryotes, bacteria initiate new rounds of DNA replication in a synchronous fashion: that is, the number of origins of replications double within a time frame that is short compared to the cell cycle duration (Skarstad et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skarstad et al., 1986.

claim: The number of origins on the bacterial circular chromosome will be of the form 2^n with n an integer.
source: This implies that the number of origins on the circular chromosome will be of the form 2n with n an integer (see Zaritsky et al., 2011) for a schematric illustration of the chromosome in fast growth conditions, and Figure 6 of Hill et al., 2012 for examples of the origin number distributions at different growth conditions).
evidence: This is an inference from synchronous initiation, supported by citations to Zaritsky et al., 2011 and Hill et al., 2012.

claim: Over a broad range of doubling times (between 20 and 60 minutes), the time from the initiation of DNA replication to division is approximately T = 60 minutes.
source: In a seminal result, Helmstetter and Cooper showed that over quite a broad range of doubling times (between 20 and 60 minutes), the time from the initiation of DNA replication to division is approximately T = 60 minutes (Helmstetter et al., 1968; Cooper and Helmstetter, 1968)
evidence: Supported by citations to Helmstetter et al., 1968 and Cooper and Helmstetter, 1968.

claim: The T = 60 minutes result is not true for slow growth conditions.
source: (note that this is not true for slow growth conditions (Adiciptaningrum et al., 2015; Wallden et al., 2016), which we do not discuss here).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adiciptaningrum et al., 2015 and Wallden et al., 2016.

claim: The Helmstetter-Cooper result was obtained using the 'baby machine', an experimental technique which approximately synchronizes the bacterial population.
source: This result was obtained using the 'baby machine' (Helmstetter and Cummings, 1964; Helmstetter, 2015), a clever experimental technique which approximately synchronizes the bacterial population.
evidence: Supported by citations to Helmstetter and Cummings, 1964 and Helmstetter, 2015.

claim: Donachie published a model linking the T = 60 minutes observation with the SMK growth law.
source: Indeed, shortly after this discovery, Donachie published an elegant model which links these two observations (Donachie, 1968).
evidence: Supported by citation to Donachie, 1968.

claim: Donachie assumed that cells grow exponentially over time.
source: Donachie assumed that cells grow exponentially over time.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption in Donachie's model.

claim: Protein synthesis increases exponentially with time.
source: Later works verified that protein synthesis increases exponentially with time (Cooper, 1988)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cooper, 1988.

claim: The buoyant mass of cells increases exponentially with time.
source: and more recently it was directly verified that the buoyant mass of cells also increases exponentially with time (Godin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Godin et al., 2010.

claim: The composition of the cytoplasm is approximately constant during the cell cycle.
source: These observations are consistent with the notion that the composition of the cytoplasm is approximately constant during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the exponential growth observations.

claim: The proportionality between cell size at DNA replication initiation and number of origins has been observed in other bacterial species.
source: This has since been observed in other bacterial species (Sharpe et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharpe et al., 1998.

claim: The proportionality between cell size at DNA replication initiation and number of origins has been directly verified in experiments where cell volume was measured at the time of DNA replication initiation.
source: and has recently been directly verified in experiments where cell volume was measured at the time of DNA replication initiation (Wallden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wallden et al., 2016.

claim: The experimental results on cell size at DNA replication initiation were done at relatively fast growth rates and do not seem to hold for slow growth.
source: Note that all of these experiments were done at relatively fast growth rates, though, and the results do not seem to hold for slow growth.
evidence: This is a caveat noted about the experimental conditions.

claim: A critical cell size for division will eliminate any correlations between cell size at birth and division, assuming a constant growth rate.
source: Assuming a constant growth rate (which is a good approximation in many cases, including E. coli in fast growth conditions), it can be shown that a critical cell size for division will eliminate any correlations between cell size at birth and division (Amir, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amir, 2014.

claim: A critical cell size for entering a new cell cycle stage which precedes division by a constant time will lead to vanishing correlations between birth and division size.
source: More generally, a critical cell size for entering a new cell cycle stage which precedes division by a constant time (as in Donachie's model) will also lead to vanishing correlations between birth and division size
evidence: This is a generalization of the previous claim, based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: In E. coli, significant and reproducible correlations between cell size at birth and division have been measured.
source: This prediction is in sharp contrast to numerous experimental findings on E. coli (Koppes et al., 1980; Osella et al., 2014; Campos et al., 2014; Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015; Soifer et al., 2016), where such correlations were measured and found to be significant and reproducible.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: A cell that was born smaller than average by a volume ΔV will also be smaller than average by the same amount at division.
source: In fact, these suggested that a cell that was born smaller than average by a volume Δ⁢V, will also be smaller than average by the same amount at division: in other words, when pooling all cells of a given size at birth together, their average size at division is related to that at birth by the quantitative law Vb=Vd+Δ.
evidence: This is based on experimental findings from the cited studies.

claim: The adder model implies that a cell 'attempts' to add a constant volume from birth to division.
source: This law may, once again, be interpreted at the single-cell level as implying that a cell 'attempts' to add a constant volume from birth to division: that is, it implies that the cue for division is the accumulation of sufficient volume from cell birth. This scenario is referred to as the incremental or adder model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: A model has been proposed in which a constant surface area is added between birth and division.
source: Recent work proposed a similar model, in which a constant surface area is added between birth and division (Harris and Theriot, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris and Theriot, 2016.

claim: A model where volume is added between two DNA replication initiation events recovers identical correlations between the various cell cycle events while reproducing the exponential dependence of size on growth-rate.
source: Such a model recovers identical correlations between the various cell cycle events (Ho and Amir, 2015), while at the same time reproducing the exponential dependence of size on growth-rate, and hence is consistent with Donachie's observations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ho and Amir, 2015.

claim: Sompayrac and Maaloe, 1973 provide a hypothetical model where an 'initiator' protein is accumulated as the cell volume grows, and initiation of DNA replication occurs when sufficient copies of that initiator are accumulated.
source: Sompayrac and Maaloe, 1973 provide a hypothetical model where an 'initiator' protein is accumulated as the cell volume grows, and where initiation of DNA replication occurs when sufficient copies of that initiator are accumulated, thereby providing a proof-of-principle that a cell may indeed add a constant volume increment without measuring its absolute size at any point in time.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sompayrac and Maaloe, 1973.

claim: The Sompayrac and Maaloe model assumes that the accumulation of the initiator does not depend on the status of the chromosome, but only on the increase in volume.
source: Note that this model assumes that the accumulation of the initiator does not depend on the status of the chromosome, but only on the increase in volume: this is accomplished by a mechanism involving two genes on the same operon.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the model.

claim: In the Sompayrac and Maaloe model, the first gene encodes an autorepressing protein whose concentration will be fixed and independent of growth rate or gene dosage effects, while the second is the initiator whose copy number reflects the relative increase in volume.
source: The first encodes an autorepressing protein, whose concentration will thus be fixed and independent of growth rate (or gene dosage effects), while the second is the initiator, whose copy number reflects the relative increase in volume.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the model.

claim: A model where the initiator protein localizes at some point within the cell and initiation occurs when its copy number reaches a threshold implies that the cell will add the same volume regardless of the number of replication forks.
source: in the first, the initiator protein localizes at some point within the cell, and initiation of DNA replication occurs when its copy number reaches some threshold. This implies that the cell will add the same volume regardless of the number of replication forks (Campos et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campos et al., 2014.

claim: In a model where the initiator is localized at the origins of replication, for conditions of multiple replication forks the cell has to accumulate more volume in proportion to the number of origins of replication.
source: In a related model, the initiator is localized at the (potentially numerous) origins of replication (or some locus close to it), and hence for conditions of multiple replication forks the cell has to accumulate more volume – in proportion to the number of origins of replication.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model structure.

claim: The model where the cell adds the same volume regardless of the number of replication forks does not lead to a narrow size distribution and does not lead to a stable size distribution.
source: The first model does not lead to a narrow size distribution – in fact, it does not even lead to a stable size distribution, as was first noted in 2014 (Campos et al., 2014)!
evidence: Supported by citation to Campos et al., 2014.

claim: When noise occasionally leads to a cell cycle where no initiations occur or two initiations occur, there is no feedback in the mechanism to allow the cell to recover the correct number of origins in the model where volume added is independent of origin number.
source: The reason for this is that when the noise occasionally leads to a cell cycle where no initiations occur – or two initiations occur – there is no feedback in the mechanism to allow the cell to recover the correct number of origins.
evidence: This is an explanation for why the model fails, based on logical reasoning.

claim: The 'adder per origin' model leads to stable size distributions and appears to explain all experimental findings discussed.
source: However, the second model (Ho and Amir, 2015), which we refer to as the 'adder per origin' model, leads to stable size distributions, and appears to explain all experimental findings discussed above.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ho and Amir, 2015.

claim: The adder per origin model provides the necessary feedback to recover from a faulty cell cycle not having a single initiation event.
source: This seemingly innocuous change of the model of Campos et al., 2014 is what provides the necessary feedback to recover from a faulty cell cycle not having a single initiation event.
evidence: This is an explanation of why the adder per origin model is superior.

claim: Biophysical models based on inhibition rather than accumulation of a protein are mathematically equivalent to the accumulation model and can also implement the incremental model.
source: While this is a possible mechanism, it is not the only way to implement this phenomenological model; in fact, it can be shown that other biophysical models based on inhibition rather than accumulation of a protein are mathematically equivalent and can also implement the incremental model (Soifer et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Soifer et al., 2016.

claim: The phenomenological observation of the 'adder per origin' model cannot unveil the structure of the particular molecular network that operates in vivo.
source: thus the phenomenological observation of the 'adder per origin' model cannot unveil the structure of the particular molecular network that operates in vivo.
evidence: This is a logical conclusion about the limitations of phenomenological models.

claim: The inhibition-based model was first proposed by Pritchard et al., 1969 and provided the inspiration for the accumulation-based model.
source: Interestingly, it is the inhibition-based model that was first proposed (Pritchard et al., 1969), and provided the inspiration for the accumulation-based model.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pritchard et al., 1969.

claim: The adder per origin model regulates the number of multiple replication forks.
source: The adder per origin model has another appealing feature – it regulates the number of multiple replication forks.
evidence: This is a property of the model based on its structure.

claim: If the cell has the wrong number of origins of replication for the given growth condition, the number of replication forks will automatically adjust until the appropriate number is achieved.
source: If the cell has the wrong number of origins of replication for the given growth condition, the number of replication forks will automatically adjust until the appropriate number is achieved.
evidence: This is a consequence of the adder per origin model's regulatory mechanism.

claim: If a cell has too many origins of replication, the accumulation of the initiator at each origin will slow down, and the frequency of initiation will decrease until the number of origins per cell reaches the correct value.
source: If a cell has too many origins of replication, the accumulation of the initiator at each origin will slow down (since the volume increment is effectively divided between all origins of replication), and hence the frequency of initiation will decrease until the number of origins per cell reaches the correct value.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation of how the model self-corrects.

claim: Within the adder per origin model, both the number of origins and cell size scale exponentially with the growth rate and are proportional to each other.
source: Within this model, both the number of origins and cell size scale exponentially with the growth rate, and hence are proportional to each other.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the model.

claim: In steady-state growth bacteria must have an exponential dependence of origin number on growth rate in order to guarantee that DNA replication will not become a bottleneck for cell proliferation.
source: in steady-state growth bacteria must have an exponential dependence of origin number on growth rate (Bremer and Churchward, 1977; Ho and Amir, 2015), in order to guarantee that DNA replication will not become a bottleneck for cell proliferation – which is why multiple replication forks presumably evolved in the first place.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bremer and Churchward, 1977 and Ho and Amir, 2015.

claim: The number of origins is an integer power of 2 in every cell, but the exponential dependence is a result of averaging over the entire population and is not restricted to take integer values.
source: (Note that although the number of origins is an integer power of 2 in every cell, the aforementioned exponential dependence is a result of averaging over the entire population and thus is not restricted to take integer values).
evidence: This clarifies how population-level and single-cell observations relate.

claim: Changing the exponential dependence of origin number on growth rate will have significant consequences on fitness.
source: Changing this dependence will no doubt have significant consequences on fitness.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary importance of the relationship.

claim: Changes in cell size by tens or hundreds of percent do not have any measurable effect on the doubling time.
source: Yet changes in cell size do not have that effect, and we may change cell size by tens or hundreds of percent without any measurable effect on the doubling time (which can typically be determined to accuracy within a few percent).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the following sentences.

claim: Thymine-limitation slows down the replication rate, extends the C period, and leads to significantly larger cells with unperturbed doubling times.
source: For instance, thymine-limitation slows down the replication rate: this extends the duration of DNA replication, which is known as the C period, and leads to significantly larger cells with unperturbed doubling times (Pritchard and Zaritsky, 1970; Zaritsky and Pritchard, 1973; Zaritsky et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In ftsZ mutants the D period is changed, leading to changes in the cell volume but not changing the doubling time.
source: Similarly, in ftsZ mutants the time between termination of replication and cell division (known as the D period) is changed: this leads to changes in the cell volume but does not change the doubling time (Palacios et al., 1996; Hill et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The control mechanism for multiple replication forks may have evolved not to tightly control size but as a means to control the number of multiple replication forks.
source: This raises the possibility that this control mechanism evolved in the first place not in order to tightly control size but, rather, as a means to control the number of multiple replication forks.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the evolutionary significance.

claim: Within the adder per origin model, the exponential dependence of cell size on growth rate is not an adaptation but a causal consequence of the regulation scheme.
source: Within this model, the exponential dependence of cell size on growth rate is not an adaptation of any sort but, rather, is a causal consequence of this particular regulation scheme.
evidence: This is the main theoretical claim of the manuscript.

claim: Many mutations affect cell size.
source: It is known that many mutations affect cell size (Chien et al., 2012; Yao et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chien et al., 2012 and Yao et al., 2012.

claim: In Lenski's laboratory evolution experiments, bacteria are grown over thousands of generations and their fitness is observed to continuously increase over time.
source: A different class of experiments where this idea can be tested are the laboratory evolution experiments pioneered by Lenski and co-workers, in which bacteria are grown over thousands of generations, and their fitness is observed to continuously increase over time (Lenski and Travisano, 1994; Lenski and Mongold, 2000; Lenski, 2004; Wiser et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple Lenski papers.

claim: In Lenski's evolution experiments, fitness should be strongly correlated with the growth rate and inversely proportional to the doubling time.
source: In these experiments fitness should be strongly correlated with the growth rate, and inversely proportional to the doubling time (this would be precise in the case where cell growth is in exponential phase and is not affected by growth of other cells in the culture).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on the experimental conditions.

claim: In Lenski's evolution experiments, together with the fitness increase, cell size also increases.
source: It is observed that together with the fitness increase, cell size also increases, see Figure 2.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2, which shows data from Lenski and Travisano, 1994.

claim: According to the adder per origin model, the increase in cell size during Lenski's evolution experiments is not an adaptation to the growth conditions but a causal consequence of the increase in growth rate.
source: According to our model, this is not an adaptation of the cell to the growth conditions, but a causal consequence of the increase in growth rate, which is presumably what is being selected for.
evidence: This is the author's interpretation of the evolution experiment results.

claim: The growth rate is expected to be under strong selection, but not T.
source: Note that we expect the growth rate to be under strong selection, and not T.
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary selection pressures.

claim: T affects the number of DNA replication forks but should not have much impact on the growth rate, since the essence of multiple replication forks is in bypassing the constraint imposed by DNA replication on the cell's doubling time.
source: While the latter affects the number of DNA replication forks, it should not have much impact on the growth rate – since the essence of multiple replication forks is precisely in bypassing the constraint imposed by DNA replication on the cell's doubling time.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the function of multiple replication forks.

claim: Previous results suggest that T might even increase over time in Lenski's evolution experiments.
source: It would be interesting to study the dynamics of the duration T in these evolution experiments, which previous results suggest might even increase over time (Mongold and Lenski, 1996), enhancing further the effect on cell size.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mongold and Lenski, 1996.

claim: The main constraints on the cell cycle architecture in fast growing bacteria stem from the necessity of correctly controlling the number of multiple replication forks.
source: Although it is intuitive to put bacterial cell size center stage in light of the various quantitative laws which it has been shown to follow, we suggest here a different view, that the main constraints on the cell cycle architecture, in fast growing bacteria, stem from the necessity of correctly controlling the number of multiple replication forks.
evidence: This is the central thesis of the manuscript.

claim: The adder per origin model is able to reconcile observations regarding the bacterial cell size which a priori seem to be contradictory.
source: The model is able to reconcile observations regarding the bacterial cell size which a priori seem to be contradictory.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the model.

claim: The adder per origin model regulates not only size but also the number of replication forks, allowing the cell to efficiently proliferate in differing environmental conditions.
source: Importantly, the very same model regulates not only size, but also the number of replication forks – allowing the cell to efficiently proliferate in differing environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a claim about the dual function of the model.

claim: Cell size correlations similar to those seen in bacteria have also been observed in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Cell size correlations similar to those seen in bacteria have also been observed in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Soifer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Soifer et al., 2016.

claim: Recent work enhances our molecular-level understanding of cell size control in budding yeast.
source: In the case of budding yeast, recent work enhances our molecular-level understanding of cell size control (Schmoller et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmoller et al., 2015.

claim: Some progress was made relating the molecular mechanism of cell size control in budding yeast to phenomenological models.
source: and some progress was made relating this molecular mechanism to phenomenological models (Soifer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Soifer et al., 2016.

claim: Budding yeast cell volume is dependent on the growth rate.
source: It is also known that budding yeast cell volume is dependent on the growth rate (Tyson et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tyson et al., 1979.

claim: The numerous differences between the eukaryotic and bacterial cell cycles suggest that a different kind of spandrel might be needed to elucidate the dependence of yeast cell volume on growth rate.
source: The numerous differences between the eukaryotic and bacterial cell cycles (for instance, that initiation occurs from many origins on each chromosome, asynchronously) suggests that a different kind of spandrel – yet to be determined – might be needed to elucidate this observation.
evidence: This is a speculation about extending the spandrel concept to yeast.

claim: A critical cell size for division eliminates correlations between cell size at birth and division because a cell born smaller than average will take longer to reach the threshold size but will not systematically divide smaller than average.
source: More generally, a critical cell size for entering a new cell cycle stage which precedes division by a constant time (as in Donachie's model) will also lead to vanishing correlations between birth and division size, i.e., a cell that is born smaller than average will take longer to reach that threshold size, but there will be no systematic bias for it to divide smaller than average – the memory of the initial conditions is 'washed away' by thresholding.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation of why the sizer model eliminates correlations.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between mother and daughter cell sizes at birth can be used to test models of cell size control.
source: For instance, one may consider the Pearson correlation coefficient between mother and daughter cell sizes at birth (Amir, 2014); this coefficient is defined as the average of the product of the fluctuations of two variables around their means, normalized by the product of their standard deviations.
evidence: This is implied by the discussion of using correlations to distinguish between models.

claim: The value of α can be determined from single-cell level correlations.
source: Its value can be determined from single-cell level correlations (Amir, 2014; see Marantan and Amir, 2016 for a recent generalization of this phase diagram).
evidence: Supported by citations in the figure caption.

claim: The prevailing model for a critical size at initiation is effectively a 'sizer' and is inconsistent with recent experimental data supporting an 'adder'.
source: The prevailing model for a critical size at initiation is effectively a 'sizer', and is inconsistent with recent experimental data supporting an 'adder'.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption.

claim: E. coli cells evolving in a culture tube show both increasing fitness over time as well as increasing size.
source: E. coli cells evolving in a culture tube show both increasing fitness over time as well as increasing size.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: The increase in both fitness and size in evolving E. coli can be naturally explained by a simple, specific regulation strategy consistent with additional experiments.
source: This can be naturally explained by a simple, specific regulation strategy, consistent with additional experiments.
evidence: This is the author's interpretation stated in the Figure 2 caption.

claim: Figure 2 is adapted from Lenski and Travisano, 1994.
source: Figure adapted from Lenski and Travisano, 1994, with permission.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption.
